stem: What happens when glucose is treated with: \(\text{a}\). Bromine water \(\text{b}\). Dilute nitric acid \(\text{c}\). Hydrogen cyanide (\(\text{HCN}\)).
solution:
Glucose is an aldohexose, \(\mathrm{CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\) : one formyl group at C-1, four secondary hydroxyl groups at C-2 to C-5 and one primary hydroxyl group at C-6. Each of the three reagents attacks a different one of these groups.

**a. Bromine water.** Bromine water is a MILD oxidising agent, so it oxidises only the formyl group to a carboxyl group and leaves the chain and the hydroxyl groups untouched. Glucose is oxidised to the six carbon monocarboxylic acid gluconic acid :

\(\mathrm{CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\) (glucose) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{COOH-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\) (gluconic acid)

Oxidation by so mild a reagent, and without loss of a carbon atom, is what shows that the carbonyl group of glucose is aldehydic, that is, a formyl group.

**b. Dilute nitric acid.** Dilute \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) is a stronger oxidising agent. It oxidises the formyl group at C-1 and the primary alcoholic \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) group at C-6, both to carboxyl groups, so glucose is oxidised to the six carbon dicarboxylic acid saccharic acid :

\(\mathrm{CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\) (glucose) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{COOH-(CHOH)_4-COOH}\) (saccharic acid)

Gluconic acid gives the same saccharic acid on this oxidation, and that is what shows glucose contains one primary alcoholic group.

**c. Hydrogen cyanide.** \(\mathrm{HCN}\) adds across the carbon-oxygen double bond of the formyl group, the cyanide going to the carbonyl carbon and the hydrogen to the oxygen, so glucose gives its cyanohydrin :

\(\mathrm{CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH + HCN}\) \(\longrightarrow\) \(\mathrm{NC-CH(OH)-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\) (glucose cyanohydrin)

This addition product, like the oxime that glucose forms with hydroxylamine, is what shows a carbonyl group is present in the molecule.

stem: How many moles of acetic anhydride will be required to form glucose pentaacetate from \(2\text{ M}\) \(\text{of}\) glucose?
solution:
**(C)** 10

Acetylation replaces the hydrogen atom of a hydroxyl group by an acetyl \(\mathrm{-COCH_3}\) group, and one molecule of acetic anhydride is used up for each hydroxyl group acetylated. Glucose contains five hydroxyl groups, so it reacts with five moles of acetic anhydride to give glucose pentaacetate, in which all five hydroxyl groups have been acetylated.

For 1 mole of glucose : 5 moles of acetic anhydride.

For 2 moles of glucose : \(2 \times 5 = 10\) moles of acetic anhydride.

\(\therefore\) 10 moles of acetic anhydride are required.

Check : the product is a PENTAacetate, so the number of moles of acetic anhydride must come out at five times the number of moles of glucose. 10 is five times 2; the values 2, 5 and 2.5 are not.

The stem writes the quantity of glucose as \(2\ \mathrm{M}\). A molarity fixes no number of moles unless a volume is given with it, so it is read here as 2 moles of glucose, which is the reading under which the question has an answer.

stem: Define carbohydrates. Write reducing and non-reducing sugars?
solution:
**Carbohydrates** are polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones, or compounds which give rise to such units on hydrolysis. Glucose \(\mathrm{(C_6H_{12}O_6)}\), sucrose \(\mathrm{(C_{12}H_{22}O_{11})}\) and starch \(\mathrm{[(C_6H_{10}O_5)_n]}\) are carbohydrates. They are also called saccharides, and the name carbohydrate comes from the fact that the molecular formula of many of them can be written as \(\mathrm{C_x(H_2O)_y}\), a hydrate of carbon.

**Reducing sugars** are those sugars which still carry a free aldehydic or ketonic group, that is, in the ring form, a free hemiacetal group. The hemiacetal group is a potential aldehyde group, so it reduces Tollens reagent and Fehling reagent and the sugar gives a positive Tollens test and a positive Fehling test.

All monosaccharides are reducing sugars, glucose and fructose among them. The disaccharides maltose and lactose are also reducing sugars : in maltose the two glucose units are joined through C-1 of the first and C-4 of the second, so the hemiacetal group at C-1 of the second ring is left free, and in lactose the hemiacetal group at C-1 of the glucose unit is left free in the same way.

**Non-reducing sugars** are those sugars in which no free hemiacetal group is left, so there is nothing to reduce Tollens or Fehling reagent and both tests are negative. Sucrose is the example : its glycosidic linkage is formed between C-1 of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose and C-2 of \(\beta\)-D-fructose, so the potential aldehyde group of the glucose unit and the potential ketone group of the fructose unit are both used up in forming the bond.

stem: Explain the preparation of glucose from cane sugar.
solution:
Cane sugar is sucrose, \(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}\), and glucose is obtained from it by acid catalysed hydrolysis.

**Hydrolysis.** Sucrose is hydrolysed by warming it with dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulfuric acid for about two hours. The hydrolysis converts sucrose into a mixture of glucose and fructose :

\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} + H_2O \longrightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

(sucrose) (glucose) (fructose)

**Separation of the glucose.** Ethanol is added to the hydrolysed solution while it is cooling. Glucose is almost insoluble in alcohol, so it crystallises out first, while the fructose stays behind in solution. The solution is filtered and the crystals of glucose are collected.

The two products of the hydrolysis are thus separated by the difference in their solubility in alcohol, and the glucose is obtained pure.

stem: How is glucose prepared by commercial method? How is peptide linkage formed?
solution:
**Commercial preparation of glucose.** Commercially glucose is obtained by the hydrolysis of starch. Starch is boiled with dilute sulfuric acid at 393 K under a pressure of 2 to 3 atmospheres. The acid breaks the glycosidic linkages of the polysaccharide and sets its glucose units free :

\(\mathrm{(C_6H_{10}O_5)_n + n\,H_2O \longrightarrow n\,C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

(starch) (glucose)

**Formation of the peptide linkage.** An \(\alpha\)-amino acid carries a carboxyl group at one end of the molecule and an amino group on the \(\alpha\)-carbon. A peptide linkage is formed when the carboxyl group of one \(\alpha\)-amino acid combines with the amino group of another : the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) of the carboxyl group and one hydrogen atom of the amino group are eliminated as a molecule of water, and the carbonyl carbon becomes bonded directly to the nitrogen atom. The \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) amide linkage so produced is the peptide linkage.

For example, the carboxyl group of glycine combines with the \(\alpha\)-amino group of alanine to give the dipeptide glycylalanine :

\(\mathrm{H_2N-CH_2-COOH + H_2N-CH(CH_3)-COOH \longrightarrow H_2N-CH_2-CO-NH-CH(CH_3)-COOH + H_2O}\)

(glycine) (alanine) (glycylalanine)

stem: Name the reagent which on reaction with glucose confirms the presence of five hydroxyl groups in the glucose molecule.
solution:
**(D)** Acetic anhydride

Glucose reacts with five moles of acetic anhydride to form glucose pentaacetate, in which the hydrogen atom of every hydroxyl group has been replaced by an acetyl \(\mathrm{-COCH_3}\) group. Five acetyl groups can be taken up only if there are five hydroxyl groups to take them, so the formation of the pentaacetate is the evidence that glucose contains five \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups. The pentaacetate is a stable compound, from which it is further inferred that those five hydroxyl groups are bonded to five different carbon atoms, since two hydroxyl groups on the same carbon would not give a stable product.

Each of the other three reagents establishes a different feature of the structure of glucose. Hydroxylamine converts glucose into its oxime, and hydrogen cyanide into its cyanohydrin; both are addition products of a carbonyl group, so these two show that a carbonyl group is present. Bromine water, a mild oxidising agent, oxidises glucose to the monocarboxylic acid gluconic acid, which shows that the carbonyl group is a formyl group. Dilute nitric acid oxidises glucose to the dicarboxylic acid saccharic acid, which shows that the molecule contains one primary alcoholic group.

stem: Write Howorth projection formula of \(\alpha - \text{D} - ( + ) - \text{glucopyranose}\). Define hormones.
solution:
**Haworth formula of \(\alpha\)-D-(+)-glucopyranose.**

Glucose exists in a ring form produced by the reaction of its formyl group with the hydroxyl group at C-5, so the ring is a hemiacetal ring built of five carbons and one oxygen. Being six membered it is called a pyranose ring, and the ring form of glucose is therefore called glucopyranose. Ring closure creates a new chiral centre at C-1, the anomeric carbon, and the two arrangements possible at it give the \(\alpha\)- and the \(\beta\)-anomer.

The Haworth formula is drawn as follows.

- Draw the six membered ring as though it stood in a plane perpendicular to the plane of the paper, with the ring oxygen at the back right hand corner and C-1 at the right hand end, the carbons running C-1 to C-5 round the ring.

- The lower side of the ring is the \(\alpha\)-side and the upper side is the \(\beta\)-side.

- In \(\alpha\)-D-(+)-glucopyranose the anomeric hydroxyl group at C-1 lies on the \(\alpha\)-side, that is, it points DOWNWARDS. In \(\beta\)-D-(+)-glucopyranose it points upwards, and the two anomers differ in nothing else.

- Place the remaining hydroxyl groups by the rule that a group written on the right in the Fischer projection formula appears on the \(\alpha\)-side, below the ring, and a group written on the left appears on the \(\beta\)-side, above it. For glucose this puts \(\mathrm{-OH}\) below at C-2, above at C-3 and below at C-4.

- Draw C-6, the \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) group, above C-5. The remaining valencies of C-1 to C-5 carry hydrogen atoms.

**Hormones** are molecules that act as intercellular messengers. They are produced by the endocrine glands of the body and are poured directly into the blood stream, which carries them to the site where they act; there they keep the biological activities of the body in balance. Insulin, released when the level of glucose in the blood rises, is a hormone, and it holds that level within narrow limits.

[Syllabus note : the Std XII chapter treats three biomolecules only, carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids, and the word hormone does not occur anywhere in it. The definition given above is the standard one.]

stem: How many optical isomers are possible for glucose?
solution:
**Sixteen.**

The open chain structure of glucose is \(\mathrm{CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH}\). Of its six carbon atoms, C-1 is the formyl carbon and C-6 is the \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) carbon, and neither of these carries four different groups. The four carbons C-2, C-3, C-4 and C-5 each carry a hydrogen atom, a hydroxyl group and two different portions of the chain, so each of the four is a chiral carbon. Glucose therefore contains four chiral carbon atoms.

Every chiral carbon can have two distinct spatial arrangements of the groups around it, so a structure containing \(n\) chiral carbons can have at most \(2^n\) stereostructures, that is, optical isomers.

Here \(n = 4\), so the number of optical isomers is

\(2^n = 2^4 = 16\)

\(\therefore\) 16 optical isomers are possible.

An aldohexose can thus exist as sixteen optical isomers, and glucose is one of them.

stem: The glycosidic linkage present in maltose is _____.
solution:
**(B)** \(\alpha\)-1,4-glycosidic linkage

Maltose, \(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}\), is a disaccharide made of two units of D-glucose. The glycosidic bond is formed between C-1 of the first glucose unit and C-4 of the second, and the first unit uses its C-1 hydroxyl group from the \(\alpha\)-side, so the linkage is an \(\alpha\)-1,4-glycosidic linkage.

The hemiacetal group at C-1 of the SECOND ring takes no part in this linkage and is left free. That is the check that the linkage has been read the right way round : a free hemiacetal group is a potential aldehyde group, and maltose does give a positive Tollens test, whereas a linkage joining the two anomeric carbons would have used up both hemiacetal groups and left a non-reducing sugar, as it does in sucrose.

stem: Write chemical reaction for the preparation of glucose from sucrose. Write structure of D-ribose.
solution:
**Preparation of glucose from sucrose.** Sucrose is warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulfuric acid for about two hours and is hydrolysed to an equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose :

\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} + H_2O \longrightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

(sucrose) (glucose) (fructose)

Glucose is separated from the fructose by adding ethanol to the solution during cooling. Glucose is almost insoluble in alcohol and crystallises out first, and the crystals are collected by filtration.

**Structure of D-ribose.** D-ribose is an aldopentose : a five carbon monosaccharide with a formyl group at C-1 and a hydroxyl group on each of the four remaining carbons.

\(\mathrm{CHO-(CHOH)_3-CH_2OH}\)

In the Fischer projection formula the hydroxyl groups on all three chiral carbons, C-2, C-3 and C-4, are written on the RIGHT of the chain, with a hydrogen atom on the left of each, the formyl group at the top and the \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) group at the bottom. The D or L configuration is assigned from the LOWEST chiral carbon, which here is C-4 : its hydroxyl group is on the right, so the sugar is D-ribose. Had that hydroxyl group been written on the left the sugar would have been L-ribose.

In the nucleic acids ribose is present not as this open chain but as the five membered furanose ring formed from C-1 to C-4 together with one oxygen atom, carrying hydroxyl groups at C-1, C-2 and C-3 and with the \(\mathrm{-CH_2OH}\) group of C-5 outside the ring. It is D-ribose that is the sugar of RNA; DNA carries 2-deoxy-D-ribose, the same sugar with no hydroxyl group at C-2.

stem: The linkage present in Lactose is _____.
solution:
**(C)** \(\beta\)-1,4-glycosidic linkage

Lactose, \(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}\), is the disaccharide present in milk. Unlike maltose it is formed from two DIFFERENT monosaccharide units, D-galactose and D-glucose. The glycosidic linkage is formed between C-1 of \(\beta\)-D-galactose and C-4 of glucose, and since the galactose unit uses its C-1 hydroxyl group from the \(\beta\)-side, the linkage in lactose is a \(\beta\)-1,4-glycosidic linkage.

The hemiacetal group at C-1 of the glucose unit takes no part in the linkage and is left free, which is why lactose is a reducing sugar. That is the check that the linkage has been read the right way round.

The \(\alpha\)-1,4-linkage belongs to maltose, in which both units are glucose and the first uses its C-1 hydroxyl group from the \(\alpha\)-side. The \(\alpha,\beta\)-1,2-linkage belongs to sucrose, in which the potential aldehyde group of the glucose unit and the potential ketone group of the fructose unit are both used up.

stem: Write preparation of glucose from sucrose.
solution:
Glucose is prepared from sucrose by acid catalysed hydrolysis.

Sucrose is hydrolysed by warming it with dilute hydrochloric acid or dilute sulfuric acid for about two hours. The glycosidic linkage between its glucose and fructose units is broken and a mixture of the two monosaccharides is obtained :

\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} + H_2O \longrightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6 + C_6H_{12}O_6}\)

(sucrose) (glucose) (fructose)

Glucose is then separated from fructose by adding ethanol to the solution while it cools. Glucose is almost insoluble in alcohol, so it crystallises out first while the fructose remains dissolved; the solution is filtered and the crystals of glucose are collected.

stem: How are proteins classified on the basis of molecular shapes?
solution:
Depending upon their molecular shape, proteins are classified into two types.

**a. Globular proteins.** The molecules of a globular protein have a spherical shape. This shape is the result of the coiling around of the polypeptide chain of the protein. Globular proteins are usually soluble in water. Insulin, egg albumin, serum albumin and legumelin, the protein of pulses, are globular proteins.

**b. Fibrous proteins.** The molecules of a fibrous protein have an elongated, rod like shape. This shape is the result of the polypeptide chains being held parallel to each other, hydrogen bonds and disulfide bonds being responsible for holding them so. Fibrous proteins are insoluble in water. Keratin, present in hair, nail and wool, and myosin, the protein of muscles, are fibrous proteins.

The difference in solubility follows from the difference in shape : a globular protein is folded with its hydrophobic side chains tucked into the interior and its polar residues on the outside, so water can surround it, while the extended parallel chains of a fibrous protein leave no such surface.

stem: What is peptide bond?
solution:
A **peptide bond** is the bond that connects one \(\alpha\)-amino acid to another in a peptide or in a protein. It is the amide linkage \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) formed when the carboxyl group of one \(\alpha\)-amino acid combines with the amino group of the next, one molecule of water being eliminated in the process.

For example, the carboxyl group of glycine combines with the \(\alpha\)-amino group of alanine, a molecule of water is lost, and the dipeptide glycylalanine is obtained :

\(\mathrm{H_2N-CH_2-COOH + H_2N-CH(CH_3)-COOH \longrightarrow H_2N-CH_2-CO-NH-CH(CH_3)-COOH + H_2O}\)

(glycine) (alanine) (glycylalanine)

The \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) group in the product is the peptide bond. The \(\mathrm{-CHR-}\) units linked by such bonds are called amino acid residues; more than ten of them linked in a chain make a polypeptide, and proteins are polypeptides having more than a hundred amino acid residues linked by peptide bonds.

stem: Write classification of proteins with an example.
solution:
Proteins are classified on the basis of their molecular shape, into two types.

| Type | Shape, and why it takes that shape | Solubility in water | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Globular proteins | spherical, the shape resulting from the coiling around of the polypeptide chain | usually soluble | insulin, egg albumin, serum albumin, legumelin (the protein of pulses) |
| Fibrous proteins | elongated and rod like, the shape resulting from the polypeptide chains being held parallel to one another by hydrogen bonds and disulfide bonds | insoluble | keratin (hair, nail, wool), myosin (muscle) |

Taking one example of each : **insulin is a globular protein** and **keratin is a fibrous protein**.

The shapes themselves are the outcome of the four level structure of a protein, the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure.

stem: What are monosaccharides? Explain denaturation of proteins.
solution:
**Monosaccharides** are the simplest carbohydrates : they do not hydrolyse further into smaller units of polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. Glucose, fructose and ribose are monosaccharides. They are the units out of which the other carbohydrates are built, oligosaccharides giving two to ten monosaccharide units on hydrolysis and polysaccharides giving a large number of them.

**Denaturation of proteins.** A protein owes its biological behaviour to a specific three dimensional shape, and that shape is held by noncovalent interactions, namely hydrogen bonds, electrostatic attractions and London dispersion forces between the parts of the folded chain. High temperature, acid, base and even agitation can disrupt these interactions. This disruption is denaturation.

Denaturation is the process by which the molecular shape of a protein changes WITHOUT breaking the amide, that is peptide, bonds which form its primary structure. So the sequence of amino acid residues survives unchanged, while the secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure is disturbed. The properties of the protein change as a result and its biological activity is often lost.

A globular protein is folded with its hydrophobic side chains in the interior and its polar residues on the outside, which is what makes it soluble in water. Denaturation uncoils it and exposes those hydrophobic regions, so a denatured globular protein becomes insoluble in water.

The familiar example is the boiling of an egg. The clear, water soluble globular protein albumin of the egg white uncoils on heating, the exposed chains aggregate, and the albumin coagulates into an opaque white solid which does not dissolve again on cooling.

stem: What is peptide bond? How is it formed?
solution:
A **peptide bond** is the amide linkage \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) which joins one \(\alpha\)-amino acid to the next in a peptide or in a protein. It is the bond that connects \(\alpha\)-amino acids to each other, and the whole chain of a protein is built of these bonds.

**How it is formed.** Every \(\alpha\)-amino acid carries a carboxyl group at one end of the molecule and an amino group on the \(\alpha\)-carbon. When the carboxyl group of one \(\alpha\)-amino acid is brought together with the amino group of a second, the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) of that carboxyl group and one hydrogen atom of that amino group are eliminated as a molecule of water, and the carbonyl carbon becomes bonded directly to the nitrogen atom :

\(\mathrm{H_2N-CHR-COOH + H_2N-CHR'-COOH \longrightarrow H_2N-CHR-CO-NH-CHR'-COOH + H_2O}\)

The \(\mathrm{-CO-NH-}\) group so produced is the peptide bond, and the product, made of two \(\alpha\)-amino acid units, is a dipeptide.

Taking glycine and alanine in that order :

\(\mathrm{H_2N-CH_2-COOH + H_2N-CH(CH_3)-COOH \longrightarrow H_2N-CH_2-CO-NH-CH(CH_3)-COOH + H_2O}\)

(glycine) (alanine) (glycylalanine)

Repeating this elimination links further \(\alpha\)-amino acids to either end of the chain. More than ten residues so linked make a polypeptide, and a polypeptide of more than a hundred residues is a protein. The end of the chain carrying the free amino group is the N-terminal and the end carrying the free carboxyl group is the C-terminal, so the two ends of the chain are not identical.

stem: Which of the following vitamins is water soluble?
solution:
Vitamins are classified into two groups according to their solubility.

**Fat soluble vitamins** are the vitamins soluble in fats and oils but insoluble in water. These are vitamins A, D, E and K, and they are stored in the liver and in the adipose, that is fat storing, tissues.

**Water soluble vitamins** are the vitamins of the B group together with vitamin C. They must be supplied regularly in the diet, because they are readily excreted in the urine and cannot be stored in the body.

Measured against this classification, the four alternatives printed with this question do not yield a single answer. Vitamin A and vitamin D are both fat soluble, so neither of them can be chosen. But vitamin C is water soluble, and the vitamins of the B group are water soluble as well, so the vitamin C alternative and the vitamin B alternative are BOTH correct as printed, and there is no ground on which one of them could be preferred to the other.

As printed, therefore, the question has no unique answer, and no key is recorded for it.

stem: What are vitamins? Name any two diseases caused by deficiency of vitamin \(\text{A}\). Write the structures \(\text{of }\): \(\text{a}\). nucleoside \(\text{b}\). nucleotide.
solution:
**Vitamins** are organic compounds required in the diet in small amounts to perform specific biological functions for the normal maintenance of growth and health of the organism. Most of them cannot be synthesised in the body and have to be obtained through food, which is why they are called essential food factors, and the deficiency of any one of them causes a specific disease.

**Two diseases caused by deficiency of vitamin A** : night blindness, and xerophthalmia, which is the hardening of the cornea of the eye.

**Structure of a nucleoside.** A nucleoside has two components, a nitrogen containing base and a five membered furanose sugar. It is formed by joining the anomeric carbon C-1' of the furanose to a nitrogen atom of the base. With a purine base, that is adenine or guanine, it is the nitrogen at position 9 that bonds to C-1'; with a pyrimidine base, that is cytosine, uracil or thymine, it is the nitrogen at position 1. Primes are used in numbering the atoms of the sugar so that they are not confused with the numbered atoms of the base. D-ribose joined to adenine in this way gives the ribonucleoside adenosine, and 2-deoxy-D-ribose joined to adenine gives the deoxyribonucleoside deoxyadenosine.

**Structure of a nucleotide.** A nucleotide is a monophosphate of a nucleoside. It is formed by adding a phosphate group to the 5'-OH group of a nucleoside, so it has three components : the furanose sugar, the base joined to C-1' of that sugar, and the phosphate group on its C-5'. Adenosine carrying a phosphate group on its 5'-OH is the nucleotide AMP, adenosine monophosphate; the same nucleotide built on 2-deoxy-D-ribose is dAMP, where the small letter d at the beginning stands for deoxyribose and MP for monophosphate. Nucleotides are the repeating monomers of which the nucleic acids are built.

[Syllabus note : the Std XII chapter treats three biomolecules only, carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids, and the word vitamin does not occur anywhere in it. The definition and the two deficiency diseases given above are the standard ones.]

stem: Which of the following is \(\text{NOT}\) present in \(\text{DNA}\)?
solution:
**(D)** Uracil

Five nitrogen containing bases occur in the nucleic acids. Three of them have a single ring and are derived from the parent compound pyrimidine, namely cytosine, uracil and thymine; two have two fused rings and are derived from the parent compound purine, namely adenine and guanine.

These five are not shared equally between the two nucleic acids. Uracil occurs only in RNA, and thymine occurs only in DNA, while adenine, guanine and cytosine occur in both. So DNA contains 2-deoxy-D-ribose with the bases A, G, C and T, and RNA contains D-ribose with the bases A, G, C and U.

Adenine, guanine and cytosine are therefore all present in DNA, and uracil is the one base among the four printed that is not.

A check : in the DNA double helix adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds and guanine pairs with cytosine through three, so every base of DNA is accounted for by those two complementary pairs, and there is no partner in the helix for uracil.

stem: Define complex lipids. Mention any two functions of lipids.
solution:
**Complex lipids**, also called compound lipids, are esters of fatty acids with an alcohol which give, on hydrolysis, one or more further groups in addition to the fatty acid and the alcohol : a phosphate group, a nitrogen containing base, or a carbohydrate. Phospholipids, in which the additional groups are phosphoric acid and a nitrogenous base, and glycolipids, in which the additional group is a carbohydrate, are complex lipids.

They are distinguished in this way from the simple lipids, the fats, oils and waxes, which give nothing on hydrolysis except a fatty acid and an alcohol.

**Two functions of lipids.**

1. **They are the concentrated energy store of the body.** The oxidation of one gram of fat releases more than twice the energy released by the oxidation of one gram of carbohydrate, so a large quantity of energy is held in a small mass of tissue and is drawn upon when the supply of carbohydrate falls short.

2. **They are the structural material of cell membranes.** A phospholipid molecule has a water attracting head and two water repelling hydrocarbon tails, and this is what makes such molecules line up into the bilayer which forms the boundary of a cell and of the structures within it.

Lipids also serve the body as a thermal insulator and as a cushion for the internal organs, and they are the carriers of the fat soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

[Syllabus note : the Std XII chapter treats three biomolecules only, carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids. Lipids appear in it in a single introductory sentence, "Lipids are the main ingredient of vegetable oils and milk fats", and no class of lipid is defined there. The definition and the functions given above are the standard ones.]
